### Problem: Maximum height by stacking cuboids {#sec-lis-p2-cube}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given `n` cuboids, `cuboids[i] = [width, length, height]`. You may rotate a cuboid so that any side is the height. You may stack cuboid `i` on cuboid `j` when `width[i] <= width[j]`, `length[i] <= length[j]`, and `height[i] <= height[j]`. Return the maximum height of a stack. A stack's height is the sum of the heights you chose.

$1 \le n \le 100$. On $[[50, 45, 20], [95, 37, 53], [45, 23, 12]]$ the answer is 190, the heights $45 + 50 + 95$. On $[[38, 25, 45], [76, 35, 3]]$ the answer is 76: the two boxes cannot share a stack. Six copies of $[7, 11, 17]$, one per permutation of the input, sum to $102 = 6 \times 17$.

Source: [LC 1691 · Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-height-by-stacking-cuboids/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Rotation means you choose which side stands up. Sorting the three sides of a box and always using the largest as the height does not lose an optimal stack: if a box can sit under another in some orientation, it can sit under it after both have been sorted. Once every box is sorted, sorting the boxes themselves puts smaller bases first, and the stack is a weighted chain under $\le$ on all three coordinates.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **Normalise.** Replace each cuboid by its sides in non-decreasing order. The height added later is the last coordinate.
- **Order.** Sort the cuboids lexicographically.
- **State.** $dp[i]$ = tallest stack whose bottom box is $i$.
- **Transition.** $dp[i] = h[i] + \max\{dp[j] : j < i,\ \text{all three sides of } j \le \text{those of } i\}$, or just $h[i]$ when nothing fits under it.
- **Answer.** $\max_i dp[i]$.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why sorting each box is a legal rotation"}
A box can be placed under another only when its three sides are componentwise at most the other's, after you assign which side is which. Sorting both triples puts the smallest side against the smallest, the middle against the middle, and the largest against the largest. If any assignment worked, this one works, and the height you add is the largest side. Equals are allowed: six identical boxes stack, and the height is six times the largest side.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
Normalise and sort. `f(i)` is the tallest stack with bottom box `i`. It adds this box's height to the best stack that fits strictly under it in the sorted order, or it is a stack of this box alone.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("cube", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "190"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: cube-rec
def _boxes(cuboids):
    boxes = [tuple(sorted(c)) for c in cuboids]
    boxes.sort()
    return boxes

def cube_rec(cuboids):
    boxes = _boxes(cuboids)

    def f(i):
        best = boxes[i][2]
        for j in range(i):
            if all(boxes[j][t] <= boxes[i][t] for t in range(3)):
                best = max(best, f(j) + boxes[i][2])
        return best

    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(boxes)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long cubeRec(int i, const vector<array<int, 3>>& b) {
    long long best = b[i][2];
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j) {
        bool ok = true;
        for (int t = 0; t < 3; ++t) ok = ok && b[j][t] <= b[i][t];
        if (ok) best = max(best, cubeRec(j, b) + b[i][2]);
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
One stored height per bottom box. The fit test is unchanged. $n \le 100$, so the quadratic scan is the whole problem.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "190"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: cube-memo
def cube_memo(cuboids):
    boxes = _boxes(cuboids)
    memo = [-1] * len(boxes)

    def f(i):
        if memo[i] < 0:
            best = boxes[i][2]
            for j in range(i):
                if all(boxes[j][t] <= boxes[i][t] for t in range(3)):
                    best = max(best, f(j) + boxes[i][2])
            memo[i] = best
        return memo[i]

    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(boxes)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long cubeMemo(int i, const vector<array<int, 3>>& b, vector<long long>& memo) {
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    long long best = b[i][2];
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j) {
        bool ok = true;
        for (int t = 0; t < 3; ++t) ok = ok && b[j][t] <= b[i][t];
        if (ok) best = max(best, cubeMemo(j, b, memo) + b[i][2]);
    }
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Table

::: {.form-next}
`dp[i]` starts as this box alone. Every earlier box that fits underneath offers `dp[j] + height[i]`. The answer is the maximum in the row. A box that fits under nothing stays at its own height, which is how the second sample returns 76.
:::

```{python}

    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: cube-tab
def cube_tab(cuboids):
    boxes = _boxes(cuboids)
    dp = [b[2] for b in boxes]
    for i in range(len(boxes)):
        for j in range(i):
            if all(boxes[j][t] <= boxes[i][t] for t in range(3)):
                dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + boxes[i][2])
    return max(dp)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long cubeTab(vector<array<int, 3>> b) {
    for (auto& box : b) sort(box.begin(), box.end());
    sort(b.begin(), b.end());
    int n = b.size();
    vector<long long> dp(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) dp[i] = b[i][2];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j) {
            bool ok = true;
            for (int t = 0; t < 3; ++t) ok = ok && b[j][t] <= b[i][t];
            if (ok) dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + b[i][2]);
        }
    return *max_element(dp.begin(), dp.end());
}
```
:::

#### Sorted chain

::: {.form-next}
The table is already the chain. This button checks the rotation on the six writings of one box: after sorting, they are the same triple, equals may stack, and six heights of 17 sum to 102. The second sample's two sorted triples are incomparable, so the answer stays the taller box.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: cube-sort
def cube_rot(cuboids):
    return cube_tab(cuboids)

one = [[50, 45, 20], [95, 37, 53], [45, 23, 12]]
assert cube_rec(one) == cube_memo(one) == cube_tab(one) == cube_rot(one) == 190
assert cube_tab([[38, 25, 45], [76, 35, 3]]) == 76
six = [[7, 11, 17], [7, 17, 11], [11, 7, 17], [11, 17, 7], [17, 7, 11], [17, 11, 7]]
assert cube_tab(six) == 102
assert cube_tab([[7, 11, 17]]) == 17
```

##### C++

```cpp
int maxHeight(vector<vector<int>>& cuboids) {
    for (auto& c : cuboids) sort(c.begin(), c.end());        // longest side becomes the height
    sort(cuboids.begin(), cuboids.end());
    int n = cuboids.size(), best = 0;
    vector<int> dp(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        dp[i] = cuboids[i][2];
        for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
            if (cuboids[j][0] <= cuboids[i][0] && cuboids[j][1] <= cuboids[i][1] && cuboids[j][2] <= cuboids[i][2])
                dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + cuboids[i][2]);
        best = max(best, dp[i]);
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
Every form sorts in $O(n \log n)$ and then spends $O(n^2)$ on the chain. $n \le 100$. The recursion is safe at that size only with memoisation; the table is the form to keep. Heights sum to at most $100 \times 10^9$, so the accumulator is a 64-bit integer.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One cuboid: its height is the largest side.
- Two cuboids that are incomparable after sorting: the taller largest-side.
- Identical cuboids stack. The comparison is $\le$, not $<$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Forgetting to sort the three sides. The input order of width, length, and height is not an orientation you are stuck with.
- Using a strict comparison. Equals may stack. Six copies of $[7, 11, 17]$ answer 102, and a strict test answers 17.
- Returning `dp[n - 1]`. A later box can be a poor base. The second sample's shorter box can sit last and must not hide the 76.
:::

**Variants.** Two keys, age and score, with the score as the weight: sort by age and take a non-decreasing score chain: [LC 1626 · Best Team With No Conflicts](https://leetcode.com/problems/best-team-with-no-conflicts/){difficulty="Medium"}. One key per row and a fixed column order is the same chain, and the answer is the width minus the longest kept run of columns: [LC 960 · Delete Columns to Make Sorted III](https://leetcode.com/problems/delete-columns-to-make-sorted-iii/){difficulty="Hard"}.
